WFP Burkina 
May 2026 
Contact info: Liam Wylie (liam.wylie@wfp.org) 
Country Director: ai Aline SAMU (aline.samu@wfp.org) 
 
WFP BURKINA FASO 
COUNTRY BRIEF 
May 2026 
KEY HIGHLIGHTS 
• In April, WFP assisted 415,351 people, delivering 
3,590 mt of food. This reflects a slight decrease 
compared to March, mainly due to operational 
constraints, while efforts continued to reach 
vulnerable populations. 
• Humanitarian needs remain significant, 
underscoring the importance of sustained 
assistance to protect vulnerable populations and 
consolidate recent gains. 
• WFP continues an integrated response across 
food assistance, nutrition, school meals and 
resilience, requiring USD 99.6 million for May–
October 2026 to sustain operations and avoid 
further deterioration in food security. 
IN NUMBERS 
 
415 351 people assisted in April 2026

Photo Caption & Credit: WFP/Photographer Jecuthiel Yameogo 
 
SITUATION OVERVIEW 
 
• Burkina Faso faces a complex crisis driven by 
insecurity, climate shocks, and structural 
vulnerabilities. Reliance on rainfed agriculture 
heightens exposure to climate variability. Insecurity 
remains the primary driver of humanitarian needs, 
with 2 million internally displaced persons (latest 
official figure, March 2023), limiting access to land, 
markets, and essential services. 
• The preliminary results from the April 2026 national 
food security and nutrition analysis projects 1.66 
million people will face crisis-level food insecurity (IPC 
Phase 3+), including 223,000 people in emergency 
situations, during the June–August 2026 lean season, 
compared to 2.3 million in 2025. While the situation 
shows an overall improvement relative to last year, 
access constraints remain significant in several 
regions, despite localized progress observed in 2025 
such as the restoration of access to Titao and 
Barsalogho. 
• Already in 2025, funding shortfalls forced WFP to 
reduce its coverage by around 30 percent compared 
to 2024, contributing to deteriorating food 
consumption and increased negative coping 
strategies among vulnerable households. WFP 
continues to deliver an integrated response including 
emergency food and nutrition assistance, school 
feeding, resilience activities, and common services 
through UNHAS, supporting national efforts toward 
stabilization and food sovereignty.
WFP Burkina Faso Country Brief 
May 2026 
OPERATIONAL UPDATES 
General Food Assistance 
• In April, WFP distributed over 2,907 mt of food and 
nutrition assistance to 197,404 people in localities 
such as Silmague, Seguenega, and Diapaga, 
including 180 mt airlifted to localities such as 
Kantchari or Gorgadji. 
• WFP took part in two government-mandated 
convoys: one to Gayeri and another to Sebba and 
Solhan. WFP had last joined convoys to these 
locations in April 2025 and December 2024, 
respectively. 
• The main challenge remains funding constraints, 
which limit WFP’s ability to meet needs. In addition, 
two WFP airlift helicopters were unavailable due to 
operational and administrative constraints, 
significantly reducing airlift capacity and increasing 
reliance on road transport. 
Nutrition 
• WFP supported malnutrition prevention by 
assisting 855 young children and 553 women, while 
screening over 2,600 children and identifying very 
few cases of moderate malnutrition; nutrition 
awareness reached more than 4,300 people. 
• To treat moderate acute malnutrition, WFP 
provided specialized nutritious foods to over 
31,700 children and 15,600 women. 
• WFP also strengthened local production of fortified 
foods through quality audits and training for 
national producers, improving standards and 
capacity. 
School-Based Assistance 
• In April, WFP reached 236,644 students (56 percent 
girls) with daily hot meals in 755 schools, including 
7,259 students who received take-home rations 
(THR), to support attendance and retention. 
• Under the integrated programme, 171,950 
students (56 percent girls) in 629 schools received 
hot meals, with THR provided to upper primary 
students meeting attendance criteria. Under 
emergency school feeding, 64,694 students (54 
percent girls) in 126 schools were assisted, 
including 34,484 IDPs, with support limited to on-
site meals due to funding constraints. 
• Efforts focused on programme quality and capacity 
strengthening (field monitoring, partnerships, 
kitchen construction), alongside coordination with 
partners and government, including Education 
Cluster engagement and planning for the phase-
out of emergency school feeding by end-2026. 
Resilience and Livelihood Support 
• In April 2026, WFP strengthened community 
resilience through the Food Assistance for Assets 
(FFA) programme, supporting the production of 
185 compost heaps (9 m³ each), treatment of 17 
gullies, and restoration of 86 hectares of degraded 
land. Activities also included the construction of 
2,101 improved cookstoves, rehabilitation of 14 
water ponds, seedling production, and assistance 
to 2,686 beneficiaries with 266 mt of food. 
• Through the Smallholder Agricultural Market 
Support (SAMS) programme, WFP reinforced 
livelihoods by supporting farmer organization 
targeting and delivering SBCC messaging, while 
strengthening capacities through trainings of 40 
participants (13 women) on GBV/PSEA and data 
collection, alongside project staff induction and 
technical workshops. 
United Nations Humanitarian Air Service 
(UNHAS) 
• In April 2026, UNHAS supported humanitarian 
operations through 246 flights to 27 destinations, 
serving 71 user organizations, and transporting 
1,351 passengers as well as 22.9 mt of light cargo. 
Despite limited flight cancellations, UNHAS 
maintained access to isolated and hard-to-reach 
locations, including Bourzanga, Gorgadji, Arbinda, 
Djibo, and other remote areas. 
 
FUNDING OVERVIEW 
Country Strategic Plan (2019-2026) 
 
 
Donors: 
Donors to WFP’s Burkina Faso Country Strategic Plan include 
Austria, Burkina Faso, Canada, Denmark, the European 
Commission, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, 
Luxembourg, Monaco, the Netherlands, Norway, the Republic 
of Korea, the Russian Federation, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, 
the United Kingdom and the United States of America. 
Additional support was provided by the UN Central Emergency 
Response Fund (CERF) and private donors, including the Ajram 
Foundation, Buddhist Global Relief, the Gwendolyn Sexton 
Foundation, and The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day 
Saints.

Article 5 / A Member of the United Nations against which preventive or enforcement action has been taken by the Security Council may be suspended from the exercise of the rights and privileges of mem- bership by the General Assembly upon the recom- mendation of the Security Council.

Accordingly, our respective Governments, through representatives assembled in the city of San Francisco, who have exhibited their full powers found to be in good and due form, have agreed to the present Charter of the United Nations and do hereby establish an international organization to be known as the United Nations.

related.excerpt: The charity Save the Children has angered the government with a social media post marking Keir Starmer’s impending exit from Downing Street. The organisation suggested on X that the outgoing prime minister was complicit in the deaths of thousands of civilians in the Israel-Gaza war. On Tuesday, it posted a mocked up picture of a commemorative blue plaque, which read: “History will not forget complicity. Keir Starmer witnessed 73,000 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces, including 21,000 children, and kept supplying arms to Israel.” Starmer’s government placed some restrictions on arms sales to Israel in 2024, but stopped short of a complete suspension. Save the Children’s X post had been viewed more than 300,000 times by Wednesday afternoon. Gaza’s health ministry said this week that more than 73,000 Palestinians have died since the beginning of the conflict on 7 October 2023, after Hamas attacked Israel. The death toll included 1,000 people who had been killed since the start of a ceasefire in October last year, according to the ministry. related.excerpt: Donald Trump has taken the war with Iran into a new, murkier phase as the two sides move further and further from the vague memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed on 17 June. And as during the opening phase of the conflict, the US leader’s objectives and methods are clouded in confusion, daily U-turns and boasts that within hours are revealed to be false. Washington’s short-term aim is clear enough – to regain control of the strait of Hormuz from Iran – and the president seems willing to extend the bombing campaign from beyond Iran’s southern shores to achieve this. But the resumed fighting is also likely to push oil prices towards $90 a barrel, potentially taking Trump closer to defeats at the US midterm elections that could bequeath him a final two years as a lame, if angry, duck. In a sign of the strategic chaos, Trump proposed – then almost immediately abandoned – a suggestion that the US could charge tolls for clearing the strait, leaving it unclear if Washington had any vision for the future of the waterway. related.title: First the coast guard, then an ICBM: China tests new, long-term ways to hold off rivals in Asia
related.summary: “That China uses the coast guard instead of the navy and air force is probably to reduce the threat profile of the exercises, so as to be able to claim restraint rather than escalating to the level of the formal military,” said Brian Hioe, a non-resident fellow at the Taiwan Research Hub of the University of Nottingham. China’s initial patrols responded to maritime boundary negotiations between Japan and the Philippines, both of which are near Taiwan, experts said.
bullets: “That China uses the coast guard instead of the navy and air force is probably to reduce the threat profile of the exercises, so as to be able to claim restraint rather than escalating to the level of the formal military,” said Brian Hioe, a non-resident fellow at the Taiwan Research Hub of the University of Nottingham.
China’s initial patrols responded to maritime boundary negotiations between Japan and the Philippines, both of which are near Taiwan, experts said.

Taiwan and Japan, maritime neighbors and historic de-facto allies, may respond with their own coast guards, Hioe said, while the United States could carry out “freedom of navigation” operations with other militaries in the Asia Pacific.

The rotation between two vessel formations on July 4, China’s description of the mission as a sustained one and its stated intent to keep strengthening patrols “all point in one direction”, said Sophie Wushuang Yi, postdoctoral teaching fellow with Schwarzman College at Tsinghua University.
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council, a government ministry, said on July 4 that the vessels were violating international law and “damaging regional stability”.
related.excerpt: NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan — China sent coast guard vessels to patrol the Pacific Ocean east of Taiwan in June and weeks later test-fired a submarine-launched ballistic missile from the South China Sea to the Pacific. While the two maneuvers answered different security-related activities by U.S. allies in Asia, experts say China used both to try out new, attention-grabbing and long-term ways to deter others from challenging its territorial claims. The Chinese Coast Guard vessels in waters east of Taiwan since May are meant as police activity rather than more provocative four years of sporadic naval or air force drills around the self-ruled island that Beijing claims as its own, analysts said. China has threatened to take Taiwan by force, if needed. related.title: July 15, 10 years on: Turkiye’s will, Turkiye’s victory
related.summary: Today, Turkiye conducts a diplomacy that thinks globally but acts locally in every corner of the world by availing of several complementary political, economic, humanitarian, and cultural tools. It has been 10 years since the nefarious coup attempt of July 15 carried out by the Fethullah Terrorist Organization (FETO), which was foiled by our beloved nation’s honourable, courageous and heroic stance. Far from faltering, Turkiye emerged from that not weaker, but stronger — ushering in a new era marked by strategic empowerment.
bullets: Today, Turkiye conducts a diplomacy that thinks globally but acts locally in every corner of the world by availing of several complementary political, economic, humanitarian, and cultural tools.

This expansion is not merely a statistic, but a reflection of Turkiye’s determination to shape, not just observe, global events, prioritising regional peace and security through peaceful resolution and mediation, and regional ownership.
As our Foreign Minister HE Hakan Fidan underscored several times, dialogue and diplomacy are needed now more than ever.
related.excerpt: The night of July 15, 2016, began like any other evening—but ended as a turning point in Turkiye’s modern history. It was a night of betrayal and defiance, fear and courage, but above all, a night when the strong will of the people determined the course of a nation. The night of July 15 was etched in our nation’s collective memory as one of the longest nights but also one of the greatest epics in Turkiye’s glorious history. It has been 10 years since the nefarious coup attempt of July 15 carried out by the Fethullah Terrorist Organization (FETO), which was foiled by our beloved nation’s honourable, courageous and heroic stance. It was the Turkish nation itself that proved decisive in repelling the existential threat of July 15 – a nation that recognises no power above its own will, and that demonstrated its readiness to lay down its life in defence of its state and democratic achievements. The Turkish nation and government turned this threat into a victory. The steadfastness of its institutions and the collective will of its people transformed the darkest night into a defining moment of national resilience.
